seamen's STRIKE-STATEMENT AS TO PROGRESS OF NEGOTIATIONS
On the orders of the day:

Yesterday the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) asked me a question with reference to the present strike on the great lakes. Hon. members will no doubt be interested in receiving a report from me with respect to the efforts which have been made to deal with the strike of seamen on the great lakes and inland waters.
The Canadian Seamen's Union and the various steamship operators represented by the Dominion Marine Association entered into a collective agreement effective August 1, 1945, for a period of one year. The agreement covered wages, rates of pay for overtime, working hours and other matters. The termination clause of the agreement provided that it would remain in effect until July 31, 1946, with a reservation that changes in the agreement could be made during the currency of the agreement by mutual consent of the parties thereto. It was under this latter provision that the union had been carrying on negotiations with the employers for a reduction in the working hours from twelve to eight per day, or from a total of 84 per week to a total of 56 per week. These negotiations having terminated unsuccessfully, the Department of Labour was brought into the situation some two months ago and, after holding separate con-

Labour Conditions
ferences with the parties, has since been endeavouring to get them into agreement on this issue.
At my first conference with the operators I took the position that I could not defend the 84-hour week, and I urged the employers, and later on the union, to settle this issue by the process of collective bargaining. Representatives of the operators and the union conferred early last week in Toronto and this conference was attended by one of the senior conciliation officers of my department.
At this conference, while the operators accepted the principle of the eight-hour day, disagreement ensued as to the detailed application of the principle, and the negotiations broke off. I then arranged that a meeting between representatives of the Dominion Marine Association, which speaks for a considerable number of the operators, and the union, would be held at my office in Ottawa on Tuesday, May 28, and both parties had indicated their intention of being present. At that meeting I was hopeful that the negotiations broken off in Toronto would be resumed and that a settlement would be reached. However, on the morning of May 24, the department was informed that two union delegates, who had boarded a vessel owned by one of the operating companies, were ordered off by the master, who said that they could not discuss their business with the crew except during the lunch period. It was claimed by the union that this was a violation of their collective agreement, and ten members of the crew, of whom eight were off duty, followed the union delegates to the wharf and were then refused readmittance to the vessel.
The union alleges that this constituted a lockout and a violation of the contract. The company on the other hand takes the position that provisions existed in the collective agreement for the settlement of grievances and that these provisions should have been invoked by the union instead of the men walking off the ship. The union thereupon called a strike on the vessels of that particular company, and this action was followed on Monday of this week by orders for a general strike.
On Tuesday of this week representatives of the union and of the companies came to Ottawa as previously arranged, and since then I and officers of my department have been meeting them in. separate conferences. Matters have been developed to the point where there was willingness on the part of the representatives of the companies and the union to meet in joint conference, and late this morning I brought them together.
So far as the movement of the ships is concerned, hon. members will I am sure have 63260-1271
read various reports in the newspapers and probably would desire me to say a word in connection with the arrests that have taken place and the reports that some disturbances have occurred.
Reports of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police would indicate that such disturbances as have occurred have, in the main, been centred in Cornwall and along the forty-five miles of canal which hon. members will recall is paralleled by a highway. This creates a difficult situation for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to control. On the other hand the disturbances have not been as bad as some press statements would indicate. Such arrests as have been made were made as a result of charges laid by the individual steamship companies.
Resulting from the joint conference between the representatives of the parties this morning it was agreed:
1.	That the Minister of Labour shall hold a meeting with the larger operators and lay before them the definite proposals which have been discussed for the settlement of the dispute. This meeting is tentatively scheduled for Monday next.
2.	That to provide for a suspension of activity it was further agreed that as Minister of Labour I should issue a statement as follows:
The union agrees to allow members who are still on ships to operate them until the meeting of operators called by the minister is over, provided the operators will suspend attempts to man ships which are now tied' up because of shortage of crews until meeting tentatively called tor Monday or any continuation thereof is concluded.
I am sure all Canada will join with me in urging upon both parties acceptance of the plan of suspending action in connection with the strike in the interest of the dominion.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, last night when we adjourned we had passed item 30, conditional upon a request made by the hon. member for Haldimand that there were some questions to be asked on grading by some members not present at the time who desired information, and some questions were also to be put by those present.

I did not say anything about
those who were not present. There were members present who wanted to ask questions.
Yes, that is correct, on grading particularly, and those questions were to be asked to-day before we proceeded with this item.

I desire to ask a question of the Minister of Agriculture regarding the grading of turkeys. Some years ago a special type of turkey known as the broad-breasted turkey was introduced to Vancouver island. By selective breeding and careful feeding a superior bird has been produced, and it is now recognized that this particular type of turkey has a definite advantage in the market. The majority of turkeys are, as the minister well knows, raised on the prairies, and are the standard type of turkey, including such birds as the bronze, reds and white hollands. This is an athletic bird which spends a good deal of its mature life in roaming the range, and, by chasing grasshoppers, develops muscular legs and wings. On Vancouver island we have no range, and our turkeys do not live such an exciting or interesting life, because as soon as they have passed from childhood-or chick-hood, if one might use the expression-they are enclosed in narrow confinement; many of them are placed upon wire and spend the rest of their lives in crates. Now the range-fed turkey or standard type is brought in a few weeks before Christmas or Thanksgiving and fattened, but the Vancouver island turkey has been fed a balanced diet all through its life, and the meat grown on it is more uniform than the meat grown on the standard type of turkey. The contention of the Vancouver island turkey growers is that the meat from their turkeys is superior to that of the prairie turkeys; in fact I am told restaurant keepers claim that sixty pounds of the meat type turkey compares with one hundred pounds of the standard type turkey; and the breeders and poultrymen of Vancouver island wish to know whether they could be given a special grading, or if the existing grades, that is, special, A, B and C, could be reviewed so far as dimensions and conditions are concerned so as to give this superior type of turkey a fairer deal in the markets and so that the breeders of these turkeys might have the benefit, rather than the hotel and restaurant keepers, of having a special grading, or the condition of the existing grades, reviewed. Can the minister give me any information on that matter, and can he have the case reviewed and see that before next Thanksgiving we get a better service?
Unfortunately I have never seen the double-breasted turkey in British Columbia.
"Broad-breasted".

I have seen the doublebreasted turkey exhibited in Ottawa, at the Chateau Laurier. I am not suggesting that any of them are in the house! At the annual meeting of the poultry people, I think it was two years ago, there was a very fine exhibit of this type of turkey at the Chateau. They were there to be seen by those attending the meeting, and on that occasion I did see them. They are a very fine type of bird, and produce, of course, much more in the way of breast meat, which is the important part of the turkey, than does the ordinary turkey.
The other matter, feeding birds without allowing them to use their muscles, does not apply only to turkeys; it has been applied in a very big way in connection with ducks. Ducks are not allowed to swim if you want them to produce just what people like to eat. If turkeys are not allowed to run, that helps too; as far as the legs are concerned.
On the matter of grading, I see no reason whatever why a special grade should not be allowed for birds of that type, whether ducks or turkeys or whatever they may be, just as we have red and blue beef in cattle. I will look into the matter and see if we cannot devise something to give proper recognition to this condition.

With reference to what my colleague has just said, you do not have to go to British Columbia to get these broad-breasted turkeys. My young lad is always at me to get some of these doublebreasted turkeys. Right in Manitoba, in the Portage la Prairie district, we have one of the largest ranches, producing from eight to twelve thousand birds a year, but they are never out roaming the prairies and becoming the athletic type that the hon. member spoke of. I should like to support .his request that the minister do something in the way of providing a special * grade. These people have developed a fine specimen of bird.

SI. Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and water storage. (This does not include the costs of survey and engineering work on the Medicine Hat irrigation and Red Deer diversion projects in Alberta and the South Saskatchewan river project in Saskatchewan, which costs are to be made available from the item of $10,000,000, No. 606, Department of Reconstruction and Supply), $3,000,000.

Under this heading the discussion of the marshlands at the head of the bay of Fundy has always

Supply-Agriculture
taken place. On May 17 the minister made this statement, as reported in Hansard, page 1641:
Of course the main problem in that area is the dikeland problem, which in a sense is somewhat similar to this. I can discuss the present position in relation to that problem more effectively under the prairie farm rehabilitation vote. 1 had hopes up until very recently of being able to report to the house that we were hoping to have something done in connection with this problem but I am not so hopeful now. I shall be glad to discuss that when we come to the prairie farm rehabilitation vote.
With your permission and that of the committee I think we should deal with this subject all at one time. I do not think it will take very long. In previous years the discussion has been mixed up with discussions on the very important subject of prairie farm rehabilitation as it applies to the prairies. I feel it would be in the interest of all concerned if we could exhaust at one time what has to be said rather than have members interested in the direct vote make their remarks. I believe my colleague the hon. member for Colehester-Hants has something to say now in connection with this item.

I would like to ask the minister's kind consideration to having the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act enlarged so that it will take in eastern Canada, and include our marsh lands in Nova Scotia.- Our problem of course is not putting water on the land; it is to keep it off the land and carry it away.
I think we have said on a good many occasions in this chamber that these lands are the most fertile and productive in Nova Scotia. They are protected from the high tides by dikes which were built a long time ago, some of them as many as a hundred and fifty years ago. In the last few years we have had very high tides in the bay of Fundy, and as a result of the wear and tear of many years these dikes have gradually given way. You may ask me why they cannot be repaired just as they were built many years ago. The answer is simple. In those days there were many men in the rural communities and on the farms who were glad to work on the dikes, digging ditches to drain these parched lands, and the cost was low. To-day however you cannot get anyone in the rural communities, or at any rate very few, to go and work in the muck and mud digging ditches all day and building dikes.
There are a few places where the dikes have been kept in very good repair, but there are a great many more that had to be abandoned. The minister knows that we have not too many areas in Nova Scotia that
are good for farming, and he knows also that the resources of the province are not as great as those of many other provinces, while our farming population is decreasing to some extent. We hear a great deal about the western farmers and what a terrible time they have had, but we hear little about the hard time that our farmers have had to face. A great deal of the sustenance obtained in Nova Scotia has come from lands that were not very fertile. For many years people made a living on those farms; in fact, they did not make a living but simply existed. Very capable people grew up on those farms and went to different parts of the world and made a name for themselves, but gradually those communities had to be abandoned. There is no one living there to-day, and I assure the committee that the great shift in the population of Nova Scotia in the years has meant a considerable hardship to the province and to farming and the rural communities.
If our marsh lands have to be abandoned, where shall we stand in Noya Scotia in regard to our farms? Some people say it will take a great deal of money to reclaim many of these lands. I dare say there are some areas which it woidd not pay to reclaim, but I contend that if even half a million were appropriated each, year for a few years, together with what Nova Scotia would do in cooperation with the marsh owners themselves, such areas would soon be restored to a proper productive condition.
We are told that it is difficult to find the money for it, but it seems to be very easy to find two or three hundred millions for this or that. Sometimes I think charity begins at home, and I would ask the minister to give his serious consideration to this question so that as many as possible of our people in Nova Scotia may be kept at home and we may have a larger production, from the marsh lands and good areas where our people may make as respectable a living as possible.
We do not want our farmers to leave the province any more than the people in any other part of the country would like to see their farmers leave. We therefore ask that the minister give the matter his earnest attention. This is a mechanized age, and modern methods are required to keep these dike lands and marsh lands in good productive condition. As I have said, you cannot get men to go and dig ditches nowadays and work the way they used to on these dikes. They simply will not do it. But modern machinery and modern methods would keep these lands in good repair. Once more I urge upon the
Supply-Agriculture

minister that he consider tlhis question very seriously so that our marsh lands may be made productive.

I wish to supplement what the hon. member for Colchester-Hants has said. What we want in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick is a definite declaration of policy from the minister and the federal government as to what they intend to do with respect to providing assistance for the reclamation and drainage of these marsh lands at the head of the Bay of Fundy. It is not suggested by anyone that the federal government should do it all, but they should take the lead in conjunction with the provincial government and with the marsh owners.
The vote for western Canada, for the prairies, I am not going to oppose. I have supported it every session, and it has amounted to $20 million-two million every year during the war years, and it is being increased this year by fifty per cent. Three millions is the vote this session, and in addition there are other items purely for the benefit of western agriculture. There is item 12, $451,340, item 25, $245,520; and in the vote we are now considering it is stated that there are special appropriations out of the sum of $10 million under this vote 31, that "this does not include the cost of survey and engineering work on the Medicine Hat irrigation and Red Deer diversion projects in Alberta, and the South Saskatchewan river project in Saskatchewan, which costs are to be made available from an item of $10 million, No. 606, Department of Reconstruction and Supply."
I would point out that these expenditures are all for the west, while nothing is being done specially for agriculture on the marsh lands in the east. This subject has been before parliament on many occasions. It was before the committee dealing with rehabilitation and reestablishment. That committee heard evidence from the premiers of the maritime provinces and the ministers of agriculture, and brought in a definite report back in 1943. This is 1946. The reports were favourable. The report was submitted to the previous parliament and passed unanimously. The provincial legislatures have passed special resolutions, and nothing is done. What the people at the head of the Bay of Fundy want to know is what the minister and his department and the government propose to do with respect to this matter. If nothing is to be done, if there is no hope, we want a declaration from them in order that the provincial legislatures and the marsh owners may know what they have to do and what they

have to face. For the time being they are waiting for a lead from the federal government.
I am going to read a recommendation of the reconstruction and reestablishment committee which sat in 1943. That committee made a report on January 26, 1944, which had special reference to the maritime provinces. The report read as follows:
Your committee has given a great deal of thought to the economic situation in the maritime provinces.
I shall not read the whole ten recommendations. The second one read as follows:
Through assistance to the farming community, by the application of the provisions of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act.
What our people want to know is what is proposed to be done in connection with our marsh lands.
I have a resolution which was passed unanimously by the legislature of Nova Scotia. There is also one I believe from the New Brunswick legislature. The Minister of Agriculture of New Brunswick came up and gave evidence before this committee. The premiers of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick came up and they gave evidence.
I shall quote a few sentences from the evidence of Doctor E. S. Archibald, director of experimental farms, Ottawa, who gave evidence before the reconstruction and reestablishment committee. At page 1026 of the evidence of that committee of December 2, 1943, he said:
There are seventy thousand acres of improved marsh land, and as stated the farmers are really not in a position to rehabilitate this themselves.
I shall skip some of his evidence and go down to the bottom of the page where the following appears:
As Mr. Black knows, surrounding all the marsh lands in the upper reaches of the Bay of Fundy there are good uplands which have gone back to scrub and woods, probably in acreage twice that of the marsh lands themselves. I cannot think of a rehabilitation job that is more potent as a basis for land settlement than a broad scale approach to this question of marsh land improvement.
Doctor Archibald has given a great deal of time to this subject, and has made many investigations at the Nappan experimental farm. He said further:
When one looks at the problems of post-war settlement in the clay belt of northern Ontario of a few million acres, the grey bush soils in the three prairie provinces, the Peace River district, central British Columbia, the area adjacent to the Alaska highway, getting further and further away from the centre of population, further away from existing social services, to think of neglecting the possibility of rehabilitat-

Supply-Agriculture
ing good lands on the seashores and in the valleys of Nova Scotia appears to me to be ridiculous.
I turn to page 1027, where Doctor Archibald said:
Then I think it is up to the government to establish a real sound live stock policy. This matter of selling hay has been the ruination of marsh land, and a good sound live stock policy which ties together both the upland and the marsh land to me is the real salvation of the situation.
Doctor Archibald is a man of wide experience, and commands the confidence of agriculturists all over Canada.
I now turn to the evidence of the Hon. A. S. MacMillan, premier of Nova Scotia. He said, at page 1020:
If our marsh land is abandoned and not reclaimed and made useful to agriculture in the maritimes, you may as well wipe out any prospect of raising stock and dairy products in Nova Scotia; and if it is going to be done, it should be done now.
You could not have a stronger statement than that. A little later on he said:
It costs considerable, even if the main arteries [DOT]were open-and you know something about the" cost of opening these arteries, the cost of maintaining them, the cost of keeping open the laterals-which are just as important as the main arteries-is quite expensive; and then the cost of keeping up the dikes.
I shall not read any more from this extensive evidence. We have had many resolutions from boards of trade and municipal councils. I hold in my hand a resolution from the Cumberland county municipal association passed on January 28, 1946. It says:
Whereas several thousand acres of dikeland are in danger of being lost to the sea, several hundred acres already lost;	-
and whereas the loss of these fertile tracts cause many farms to become too small to be profitable productive units;
and whereas the main drainage vents are clogged with rushes, and sediment owing to scarcity of labour for regular ditching;
and whereas these conditions are causing a great loss in production and assessment;
Therefore be it resolved that the municipal council of Cumberland, in regular session on this twelfth day of January, A.D. 1946, hereby respectfully petition our provincial and federal governments to render early assistance.
A resolution placed on the order paper in 1946 by the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor) is expressive of the general interest of those in public life in Nova Scotia. I shall not read the preamble. The body of the resolution reads:
Therefore be it resolved,-That, in the opinion of this house, in any programme of reconstruction, rehabilitation and development, the government should take into consideration the advisability of developing that tract of marsh land, consisting of approximately 100,000 acres located
along the head waters of the Bay of Fundy in the counties of Cumberland, Nova Scotia and Westmorland, New Brunswick.
And he might have said, the counties of Colchester, Hants, Kings, Annapolis and Albert in New Brunswick.
I have another resolution from the Colchester county council. I do not wish to delay the committee by reading it all. It is a long resolution. This affects not only marshlands. How much land is involved?

If nothing is going to be done, if there is no hope, if it is against the government's policy, if there is something holding it back or preventing its making a contribution or a declaration of policy, then let the minister make a statement so that the marsh owners, the provincial legislatures and the ministers of agriculture will know what the situation is. Let me go on and I will give it to you. This question of the marsh lands has been a live issue for many years. I do not know how long it was a live issue before I came to Ottawa, but it certainly has been ever since. I understand that the hon. member for Cumberland, who has just spoken, was in the government of Nova Scotia at the time the matter first became a live issue here. This question is one of many that arise across Canada in connection with responsibility of the provinces or where a province finds itself in the position of having to do a job and not being able to find the money with which to do it.
This matter is clearly one of provincial responsibility, and it always has been. The province has legislation governing drainage, just as other provinces have similar legislation, particularly those in the west. The governments of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have found it impossible to repair the dikes, some of which were built many years ago with the assistance of governments even outside of Canada when settlers were first going into these areas. The dikes have deteriorated and it has been found most difficult to obtain funds with which to repair them, through provincial legislation, municipal legislation or otherwise.
I have not the complete history before me, but many years ago these lands fell into disuse, partly owing to the fact that an active live stock industiy which had existed in earlier days had gone backward rather than forward. The people of that area are not raising as much live stock now as they did a long time ago. Whether the fact that there had been a stoppage in the production of live stock was in some degree responsible for their not being interested in the marsh lands, or whether the fact that the marsh lands were not properly handled was responsible for live stock production going down, is a moot question. One could take either side of that question, but the fact is that the lands are not producing live stock as they once did or to the extent that they could produce.
In 1934 or 1935 an amount was placed in the estimates. This may have been done at the suggestion of the government of Nova Scotia when the hon. member was a member of that
government, or it may have been done at the suggestion of Doctor Archibald, who was then and still is the head of the experimental farms. He comes from that section of Canada and, as has been suggested, he knows this problem perhaps better than anyone else in Canada. He has always been a strong advocate of putting these lands back into production to the same extent that they were in an earlier age.
I made my first trip to the maritime provinces in 1936, the year after the vote had been placed in the estimates. The vote was to permit some work being carried on by the experimental farm down there to determine [DOT] whether or not these lands could be brought back into the production they had been capable of in an earlier day. Doctor Archibald was with me, and we went over the land together and decided to go ahead with the experiment. The experiment was conducted, and I think it was three years ago that I went back with Doctor Archibald to look at the results of the experiments. I think I can say without fear of contradiction that there was easily three times as much alfalfa growing on the land that had been properly drained and cultivated by the experimental farm as there was on land immediately across the fence. That proved to my satisfaction that this is a job that ought to be done.
We are looking for land upon which to settle men coming back from overseas, upon which to settle persons who are coming from the over-populated areas in other parts of the world, and upon which to settle the sons and daughters of our farmers in different parts of Canada who still wish to carry on in agriculture. Doctor Archibald was with me on that second visit, and I agreed with him when he said that there was no place in Canada in which a better job could be done, where money could be spent to better advantage than to take care of these marsh lands and make them produce as they are capable of producing. I think everyone who is familiar with the situation will agree with me when I say that that job ought to be done.
The fact is that there is responsibility on at least two authorities, but when we discuss the matter with the provinces they maintain and insist that there must be responsibility placed upon a third group, namely, the people who are on the land. It is all very well to say that the leadership should come from Ottawa; the fact is the leadership, with our constitution as it is, ought to come from the provincial government. There is a reason for the provincial governments coming to Ottawa and saying that we should assist, but the leadership ought to be with the provincial governments.

I am inclined to believe 'that the leadership has been with the provincial governments. They have been urging the matter and insisting that something ought to be done. I think that hon. members who have discussed the matter up to the moment might have said that something has been done. We have been operating on these lands for the last three years under an arrangement made between the provinces and the federal government. We have been spending some money-not as much .as I would like to see spent-the provinces have been advancing part and the farmers themselves have been made responsible for the payment back of some of it.
The expenditures that have been made have been only for emergency repairs of breakages in the dikes.

That is just what I was .going to say. Those are the only kind of expenditures that can and ever will be made under a three-way arrangement. It is all very well to argue that we should go to the provinces and say, "You give us fifty per cent of the cost." What will happen is that they will go to the municipalities or to the individual farmers and say, "We will spend dollar for dollar with you." It would all be based on what the farmer or the municipality could spend. The amount that the municipality or the farmer can spend, multiplied by three, will not do the job at all. We may go to start to build a dike with $100,000 or $50,000 and be able to do only half the job when the season is over. Then it is all washed out and we might as well not have spent any money at all. That is what has happened on two or three *occasions.
The position the government finally took was that this was one of a number of problems that should be submitted to the dominion-provincial conference, that there should be a decision upon it. This policy did not apply only to this particular job; it Applied to the P.F.R.A., to road building, and do many other things. I believe the hon. member for Cumberland was once minister *of highways of his province, and I was once minister of highways in my province. At the end of the last war I directed the expenditure *of Saskatchewan's part of the $20,000,000 which wTas voted for road work. Long before I got through spending that money I came to the *conclusion that we were wasting the greater part of it because of the necessity of getting undertakings between Ottawa and Saskatchewan. I venture to say we have wasted much *energy and a considerable part of the money voted for this project by the fact that we
.{Mr. Gardiner.]
must sit down and discuss it with the municipalities and provinces before anyone starts to do anything, so that by the time we get started the season has passed, and, this country being so far north, the opportunity is gone to do anything worth while. As a result of that experience I have maintained and still maintain that the job ought to be done by some one government, and that some one government ought to have control of sufficient money to do it and do it properly. If there is to be an understanding arrived at with regard to maintenance, let that be undertaken also.
But so far as doing the job is concerned, what I have been suggesting from the very beginning is that the federal government ought to recondition these dikes and clean out the main ditches-that is if we are to take on any part of the work. We should go ahead and do the main job which is to protect the land, and then someone else can do the rest of it. But my difficulty when I approach the treasury to get sufficient money to do that has been to get someone else who will take the responsibility for making use of the lands after the money has been spent. The treasury will say: What is the use of spending four or five million dollars or even two or three hundred thousand dollars blocking up a few holes and cleaning out a few ditches and taking out some rotten abutments and putting in new ones in certain places and leaving the job undone somewhere else, so that the water gets in behind and undoes all the work you have done and the expenditure you have made? Someone has to take over the job in a big way and do it in a big way and get the main part of the job done.
I had hoped when the dominion provincial conference was called that we should get this question settled this year. As has been stated, an act was drafted, in fact two acts. People who know their own problems perfectly but do not know the problems in other parts of Canada are continually making statements in this house with regard to those other parts which are unjustified. I had occasion a few days ago to say something with regard to freight rates, as related to the shipment of grain from western to eastern Canada, in defence of those who live in eastern Canada, and those who were discussing the question and relating it to the western P.F.R.A. did not really understand the position. I know what my hon. friend from northern Manitoba, who has been waiting to get into this discussion, is going to say. He is going to say that the line over which we do not go runs right through his constituency, and that a considerable part of his constituency does not come under the P.F.R.A. Every member from

But there is a good reason why the government took in the Palliser triangle. It was the Bennett government that did it, and the reason was that people had been put into that area. He said that these people ought to be assisted in getting reestablished on that land, and I agreed with him in taking that position. But hon. gentlemen will see that that * problem is entirely different from the problems in most other parts of Canada. The problem in the maritime provinces which we have been discussing existed before there was a Dominion, of Canada. It came to us when the provinces joined confederation. But the Palliser triangle problem was one which we ourselves created, and therefore Mr. Bennett said that the federal government ought to finance the reestablishment of those people who had been put in there by the federal government against the good advice of some people.
What I want to emphasize is that there is just as much opposition to applying this assistance only to the Palliser triangle in western Canada as the opposition we heard only a few moments ago from the hon. member for Cumberland to this assistance not being applied to Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. We should all get together and agree. We are not battling one another. We are not criticizing anything being done in any other part of Canada. But here is a job that ought to be done, and it requires a great amount of money which can only be provided by the federal government. This being so, we ought to do something about our constitution. In the conference, instead of talking generalities
that do not solve very much, we should try to get a question like this settled. But people like to go to these conferences, as they go to international conferences, where very often they discuss things that do not solve very much. They talk generalities. We tried to get this question before two conferences. We tried to get permission to sit as a special committee and discuss this question with the conference and make recommendations on it. But other questions were regarded as bigger and more important. I personally do not think they were bigger, but some people thought they were. The governments discussed other matters and went home and left this question entirely unsettled, as well as similar questions on which we probably could have reached agreement in a week if we had got together and discussed them instead of discussing simply theoretical questions.
As I said, I had two acts drafted. One was for the four western provinces. The name would have to be changed; it would not be prairie farm rehabilitation, but simply rehabilitation. If that bill had been passed by the house it would have covered the four western provinces. Another bill was drafted to cover the five eastern provinces. We had intended to have the administration of the act dealing with the western provinces centred where it is now, at Regina, and the administration of the other act centred at Ottawa. They deal with two completely different problems. One deals largely with drought; the other deals with too much water, and in British Columbia there is a combination of both because there are areas in that province which need diking, and other areas which need irrigation; and sometimes these areas are only five or six miles apart, depending upon' where the range of mountain lies.
These problems exist right across the country, and we believe that there ought to be agreement in the first place on certain sources of revenue being open to the federal government which are now tapped by the provincial governments in order that we may have the means to do these things. Then we ought to have a division of authority to make it possible for us to spend the money in these areas. I have been going to provincial conferences ever since 1922, and there have not been very many decisions arrived at in all that time; but I am still hopeful that while I am alive and in .politics we shall reach a decision on some of them, and if we do, I can guarantee to the hon. member for Cumberland that we shall give leadership in the problem, just in the same way as we have given leadership in connection with the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. But the first thing I had to do in

The definite action that was going to be taken was awaiting this legislation; but I have insisted, and I think the government agrees with it, that either the province or ourselves, one or the other, must take absolute responsibility for carrying on the further work there; that if we undertook the responsibility then the province must turn the money over to us and we will go ahead. If the province undertakes the responsibility then we will turn our money over to them and they will go ahead and take responsibility from that point. Whatever money is advanced is advanced, and that is the end of it. If we do things that we should not have done under arrangements with the province we shall have to pay for it. If they do the job and something happens that was not anticipated or because of the fault of anyone, then they will probably have to do the paying. I think it should be either one or the other and we should get ahead with the job and have the whole difficulty cleared up.
It is important that the work be done this coming season if it is at all possible.
I agree.
If it is not done you will have to do it all over again.

I agree with that. When I spoke a moment ago I should have said that later on in the supplementary estimates there

will be appropriations brought down either by myself or by someone else to take care of the work which must be done there, and I hope this will be brought down shortly.

I appreciate the statement of the minister, but this is an appropriation to deal only with emergent repairs. The main policy, if properly put into effect, would bring about conditions which would do away with the necessity of expenditures for repairs; repairs would not be necessary. In the last few years no work has been done until the dike is broken and the aboideau goes out. Practically all the dikes have weakened or the aboideaux have weakened; the canals and drainage ditches have filled up. JYith a general policy for new work and the money properly expended it will not be necessary to make these repairs at all. We want a general policy. I appreciate the statement of (the minister and thank him for the undertakings he has given. But the fact remains that no immediate action is being taken.
I agree with the minister that some body should be set up which would carry the responsibility. That body should have the con- . fidenee of the marsh owners and the provincial governments as well as the federal government. It might be a commission, or, as the minister suggests, it might be carried out entirely by the federal government with the provincial governments and the marsh owners making their contributions.
What we should like to have is an expenditure. of at least half a million dollars, and that it be made available this year. We should also like a policy arrived at which would be satisfactory to all concerned, and which could be carried out in the next five or ten years. That is a long-term policy. The success of agriculture and stock raising in that whole area depends on it, and that policy should be arrived at without any further delay. What is grieving these people who are interested is that this matter has been discussed and no policy has been decided on. Any expenditure that is being made is with respect to emergent repairs after the damage is done.

As the Minister of Agriculture said a few moments ago, I have been popping up and down regularly since this discussion began.. However, I understood there was some urgency in the matter of the Nova Scotia marsh lands and on this occasion I was happy to give way to the hon. members from that area who wanted to speak on it.
In the past there have been suggestions and complaints that when the estimates of the Department of Agriculture are before the committee, western members monopolize all
the time; therefore on this occasion I thought we should show our good-neighbour policy and give them an opportunity to discuss their matters.
The Minister of Agriculture was kind enough to make half of my speech for me; therefore I shall not have to burden him very long, but there are a few matters in connection with prairie farm rehabilitation with which I wish to deal. I think it is clear to all hon. members of the committee that it is not only a matter of prairie, farm rehabilitation but a. matter of rehabilitation generally across Canada.
Last fall I had a discussion with the Minister of Agriculture and brought up the question of the advisability of extending the boundaries of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. I do not know what is in the draft that the minister has prepared, but in the act as passed in 1935, and amended in 1937, 1939 and 1941, these words appear; they are the key words:
The committee shall consider and advise the minister as to the best methods to be adopted to secure the rehabilitation of the drought and soil drifting areas in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta.
Evidently the original purpose behind the act and, as it still stands, was to rehabilitate those areas which were known as the drought areas, and which are sometimes referred to as the Palliser triangle. But as the years went by it was found that there were other matters which entered into the question of drought ; that is, there were certain other areas in western Canada which were not in the drought area, but which were becoming drought areas because no precautions were being taken to conserve the water or to conserve the texture of the soil. Something of that kind is in process of taking place in the constituency I have the honour to represent. That is why I pressed the question last fall and want to do so again.
On numerous occasions several municipalities within the Dauphin electoral district have made representations to the government-I believe years before I came to the house-to be included in the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. I need only to quote from one of the resolutions to show What I mean. This resolution comes from the rural municipality of Grandview, and is in these words:
Therefore it is resolved that the rural municipality of Grandview make application to the prairie farm assistance branch of the dominion government to have the rural municipality of Grandview included in the area which qualifies for financial assistance to farmers in the making of dugouts on farms.

The minister said that on the prairies it -was mainly a problem of dealing with drought areas, and getting more moisture there, Within thirty miles of this same municipality which is appealing for assistance to make dugouts in order to obtain a supply of water we have a situation just south of the town of Dauphin where the very opposite is the trouble. There in the spring time we have flood waters which do a great deal of damage to the best farm land in Manitoba. I have already had correspondence with the Minister of Public Works and . the Minister of Mines and Resources as to where the responsibility lies for doing something to control these waters which come down from the. Riding mountain national park, which, in my opinion, and in the opinion of the municipalities concerned, makes the federal government at least- partly responsible for the flood condition. It has a double effect, because in the spring time the water rushes down; the creeks overflow the banks and destroys or damages good farming land. Within a few months, in fact within a few weeks in some years, the water is all gone; the creek beds are dry, and there is not even a supply of water for the live stock in the area. They have evolved a plan whereby a number of controlled dams can be built at a fairly reasonable cost, so that the waters, instead of coming down in the spring and drying up completely in the hot days of the summer, can be so controlled as to provide a steady flow of water all through the year. I believe it is a worthy project.
I shall have more to say about national parks on another occasion. I would point out, however, that the condition has been caused largely by the fact that the timber in the national park has been denuded. When the timber was thick the snow which fell in the winter melted slowly in the spring time, and the water was controlled by nature. Then, beaver dams kept the water in a controlled state.
But since the timber has been removed by certain interests, the water now comes down much faster, with the result that we have flood conditions. I leave this matter for the attention of the minister. In passing, may I - say I have every sympathy for those in Nova Scotia because of the condition which exists there. I know something about marsh lands.
I leave the plea with the minister that Ee ought not to delay the introduction of the measure he has drafted until agreement is reached with all the provinces. As I understand the situation, it is the break-down of the dominion-provincial conference that is delaying the introduction of the bill to incor-

porate the four western provinces under a new rehabilitation measure. I believe it will be admitted that the four western provinces which took part in the conference were willing to sign an agreement with the dominion. That being so, I can see no reason for delay in introducing a bill w'hich would formulate an agreement for those provinces which are now willing to come to an agreement.
If the eastern provinces still have differences of opinion which they think must be resolved, then they may have to wait until such time as that is done. I believe the western provinces indicated their good faith at the conference, and are willing to come to an agreement. The minister has a green light to go ahead with the introduction of the bill.

The people of the irrigated section in southern British Columbia will, I know, read with a good deal of regret the minister's statement this afternoon that, consequent upon the adjournment of the dominion-provincial conference he does not believe it will be possible to proceed with rehabilitation work in that part of British Columbia at the present time.
The minister has received a brief submitted by the association of irrigation districts in British Columbia. I certainly shall not read it, but shall point out that its object is to urge the federal government to extend to British Columbia the terms of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, so that many veterans now settling in the irrigated areas may not be handicapped by inability to find land.
I shall place only one paragraph on record, because it succinctly states the case:
There are in the Okanagan valley and immediate vicinity some 27,000 additional acres of arable land, mostly within, or adjacent to the present irrigation systems, which could be brought under irrigation at a cost of from $100 to $150 per acre. The increase in production from this acreage would eventually double the present production of the area, expand the towns to almost twice their size, and cause new towns to develop. The resultant production would provide increased employment and augment the available market for goods from the coast cities, from the prairies and from the east, just as the P.F.R.A. projects are improving our markets for fruit by assuring the prairie farmer a full crop, regardless of drought.
That states in a few words what is in the minds of farmers in the irrigated districts. The condition is not identical with the drought conditions of the Palliser triangle. But the land in the dry belt in the southern part of British Columbia is capable of producing very little in the nature of crop until irrigation water is applied to it. Then there is scarcely any limit to the crops which may be grown there.

Sup-ply-Agriculture
Once that land is developed, as a good many tens of thousands of acres have been developed over the years, not only does it carry increased * population, but it produces secondary industries. The increased population must be supplied with the necessities of life, and those requirements in turn cause business for the merchants, and freight for the railways. It is an area in which returned men are most desirous of settling. But the difficulty is that the land, so productive when irrigated, is valued at a high price. There are very few pieces of developed and irrigated land which fall within the terms of the Veterans' Land Act.
The consequence has been that endeavours have been made in the last two years to discover areas which can be irrigated at a cost that would not be too high, and which could then be turned over to veterans for purposes of settlement. There must be ten or fifteen veterans to every parcel of land which a veteran under the land act is capable of obtaining.
I have in mind three areas concerning which consideration has been given to the possibility of putting irrigation water on. The benefit of engineering advice from those connected with the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act has been received in connection with formulating schemes for putting water on the land.
I should like to learn from the minister his hopes and expectations in the -matter, and whether next year we may look to rehabilitation expansion in that part of British Columbia.

Mr. Chairman,
strange to say, I am asking, not that water be brought on, but that it be taken off. Cannot this procedure be extended to give protection to certain areas in the Fraser valley? Our trouble is that of keeping the water off, not on. We are asking only that the act be extended to protect us from flooding conditions in the river. Would the minister state whether, under the measure, we might expect to have our land protected from flood and flood erosion?

As the minister is likely to answer all our questions at the same time, perhaps I might now get in under the wire and ask one or two. I believe it would be a fine policy for some political party-I hope the Progressive Conservative party does not do it -to advocate that we export some of our drought from the west and import the surplus water from the east, thereby bringing about a greater balance.
The problem I would draw to the minister's attention is somewhat different from either the marsh lands problem in the east or the irrigation problem to w'hich reference has just been made. The. problem that arises in the Peace River block is different from either of these. In that district it usually rains sufficiently to provide them with crops and they are not troubled with floods. Their difficulty is to find sufficient water in wells for the use of their families and their stock during the summer. They are anxious to come under the P.F.RA. in order that reservoirs may be built to hold the melting snow in the spring and thus provide sufficient water for their stock during the summer. I expect that the minister's answer, at least in part, will be something similar to that which he gave in connection with the marsh lands of Nova Scotia. Last year, when the matter was under discussion the minister said that he was referring the problem to the dominion-provincial conference. Certainly the question is still under reference and has not yet been settled. I should like to emphasize the point raised by the hon. member for Dauphin, that the minister should proceed with his legislation and then have the provincial governments pass enabling legislation later on in order to carry out the work which he has in mind.

I think this act should be extended to cover those of us who-want to keep water off their land. In the Fraser valley our land is protected by dikes. In 1904 a dike broke and we built a new one which cost several hundred thousand dollars. I have had several questions about this on the order paper but I have not been able to get satisfactory answers. When the Canadian Pacific built their line running into the United States to connect with the Northern Pacific they claimed that they had built above the high-water line. They have never paid any diking tax, and the result has been that their land is protected from freshets at the cost of the farmers of the district, although at the present time their line is eight feet below the highwater mark. This branch line is one of the best paying lines in their whole system. I asked question after question about this but I was told that the government had no information. I presume the Canadian Pacific did not want to give out the information. Can the minister assure me that the farmers in my district will have every assistance in keeping water off their land? I should like to ask also if the minister can get me the information I want as to why
Supply-Agriculture

the Canadian Pacific are able to have full protection from floods at the cost of the farmers of the Fraser valley?

I think the questions which have just been asked are the best demonstration we could possibly have as to the idea that is held about what the federal government can do. The diking in British Columbia was undertaken as either a provincial or a municipal responsibility. The taxes just referred to by the hon. member would not be collected by this government. Those who replied that they had no information were making the only posible answer. If we are to start in to try to get information with regard to municipal and provincial taxes in order to answer questions I am afraid we will be very busy and we shall be attempting to keep other people very busy when we have no authority over them. I think the proper place to get that information would be the provincial government, some municipal organization or any other organization that has been set up to handle the collections having to do with diking. It certainly would not be the Department of Agriculture, because that matter would have nothing to do with these estimates. Therefore I am not in position to answer that question.
Dealing with the other matters, we should have nothing to do with diking in British Columbia unless we had special legislation such as I referred to a few minutes ago which imposed that responsibility. That special legislation probably will be forthcoming only if certain financial arrangements are made between the provinces and the federal government making it possible for some of the revenues which now go provincially to go federally. I may say that we are hopeful that some time that may happen.
When it was decided recently that this legislation would not be proceeded with this session I did ask that consideration be given to the possibility of our proceeding with works of a certain kind, under restrictions if necessary, to bring about some of the developments which we hope some day can be carried out under the type of legislation we have been discussing. One of these works is a project similar to the one referred to by the hon. member for Kootenay East.
There is one project in the Pemberton river area which I know quite well. I am not sure just when it was put in there, but a soldier settlement was put in following the last war. I do not know of any more naturally beautiful spot that that one; but unfortunately the river, which is fed from a

glacier, is quite close to the top of its banks at all times. The whole plain is built up from silt which has been carried down by the floods. All that is needed is for a tree to fall some night, as often happens, the silt form behind it to form a dam, and flooding occurs. Engineers have looked over this project and I have more details with regard to it than I have with regard to any other.
We have sent the P.F.R.A. engineers in there, and we have a report which would suggest that by blasting out some of the rock in the stream we can lower the level of the water and allow it to get away with greater readiness, and then by a certain amount of diking keep the river from flooding.
That is entirely different from the Okanagan; that is similar to the case mentioned joy the hon. member for Fraser Valley.

The Fraser is quite different from the Pemberton; it runs through a different type of country and a different situation is created. The area is much larger. One reason for being interested in this particular situation was that they are all returned soldiers. We could not take exactly the same position with regard to the Fraser river, because that country has been settled for many years and municipal organizations have been built up. We had nothing to do with putting the people there, but we cannot say that about the Pemberton area. We put the returned soldiers in there after the last war and I think we ought to do something about it as a special case.
As to these other irrigation projects, one of them is only seven or eight miles from the Pemberton valley, just over the mountains in the Lillooet district, in the constituency of the hon. member for Kamloops. There is an irrigation project which could give good results. There are similar areas in the valley where fruit is grown. Putting water on a larger area would make it possible for many more people to live and sustain themselves there. These projects could all be considered under legislation such as we had hoped to bring down this session. While a project such as the Pemberton one could be proceeded with this summer, it would be most difficult to proceed with projects in the Fraser valley or in the Kootenay district without legislation.

I think all the people of western Canada have a high appreciation of the excellent work done under P.F.R.A., specially in regard to small water projects and in regard to the surveys which have been made by the P.F.R.A. engineers in connection with larger irrigation projects.

Supply-Agriculture
I have a great deal of sympathy for the problems put before the committee by the hon. member for Cumberland. I should like to see the P.F.R.A. extended to every province. I recall that when this question was before the reconstruction committee which sat for two or three sessions, a recommendation was made to that effect. We were investigating a number of worth-while projects for the purpose of developing the resources of the country and thereby increasing the wealth of the country, and I think it was felt by the committee that these projects should be undertaken as national projects and financed by the federal government. Once the project had been constructed and completed, the maintenance would fall on the provinces and municipalities and the farmers concerned on a certain share basis.
We also discussed in the committee the problem of the salt marshes, and some of the witnesses pointed out that these salt marshes originated as a result of the farmers being unable to maintain their dikes because of depressed prices. While the maintenance of dikes may have been a provincial responsibility, to-day we all recognize that the maintenance of prices is a federal responsibility and that unless we maintain prices at a level which will meet the cost of production, it will be impossible for the farmers to carry on the necessary maintenance work. That is a good example of the devastation resulting from a depression or deflationary policy. We hear so much of the dangers of inflation, but we seldom hear of the terrible devastation caused by a deflationary policy. After the deflationary period has gone, we are left with a heavy capital depreciation, which costs many times more'than it would have cost to maintain the capital in the first place.
The main criticism I have heard in the west regarding P.F.R.A. has been that they have not expanded their work rapidly enough. I realize that that is not really a criticism of P.F.R.A., but rather of government policy, because P.F.R.A. is dependent upon government policy for the amount of work they can do. Whilst the people are critical in that Tegard, they realize the impossibility of going ahead with these large-scale projects during the war, but they feel that, now that the war is over, no time should be lost in going ahead with them at the earliest possible day. There was a good deal of disappointment visible when the Minister of Reconstruction stated that these national projects would not be [DOT]gone ahead with for two or three years, because the federal government was building up a shelf of projects to take care of unemployment in the future. However, I understand that
the government's policy has been modified so that some of these projects may be started at an early day or are now being started. It is a very good thing that the government has decided to start the work earlier, because day after day we are told of the tragic plight of people in Europe and Asia as a result of the shortage of food; and while this condition is largely, I believe, the result of the war, nevertheless it has been aggravated considerably by a number of crop failures throughout the world. This condition is not only tragic but an extremely dangerous one, because one of the main essentials of a sound peace is an ample supply of food. If we are to allow shortages of food to continue it will be that much harder to bring about a satisfactory peace in the world to-day.
This spring there was quite a general demand that we should increase wheat acreage in western Canada. The farmers were urged to reduce their summer-fallow in order to expand their sown acreage, but I think the Minister of Agriculture was wise when he advised against such a policy because the reduction of summer-fallow may easily bring about a reduction in production over a two-year period.
The only safe way to overcome drought is by irrigation. You may mitigate it by cultural practices, but in the final analysis the only way to overcome severe drought is by the application of water. In western Canada we have a number of rivers running through the parched lands and practically no use is being made of the water. We have rivers without a dam or a power project. The water of these rivers is urgently needed now to irrigate the lands in the drought areas, and no time should be lost in starting these irrigation projects, because we now have the men and, I believe, the machinery available, so that an early start could be made.
In past years-I am thinking especially of the thirties-when we discussed irrigation in this house we were met with these two main objections: first, the cost would be too great; we could not afford it; second, if we were to carry out large-scale irrigation projects we would increase the amount of farm produce and create surpluses. Dealing with the first objection, the financial cost, to-day we should realize that it is not a question of not being able to afford it but of not being able to afford not to do it. Let us consider the cost of failure to provide irrigation in some parts of the drought areas in western Canada. I shall give an example from my own constituency which no doubt could be duplicated in many other parts of the west.
Supply-Agriculture

In the constituency of Acadia, from 1918 do 1935, over $10,000,000 was paid out in direct relief, and from 1935 on many more millions have been granted in the form of seed and feed relief and under prairie farm assistance. Thousands of homes were abandoned and thousands of acres have become useless for pasture because of the lack of water.
Recently surveys have been completed by P.F.R.A. engineers of the Red Deer diversion project, which would involve an initial expenditure of $6,750,000. It would flood 1,200 miles of waterways and provide a reservoir to irrigate half a million acres and provide water for 8,000,000 acres of pasture. It would take probably another $7,000,000 to get the water from the reservoir on to the land. That cost, I take it, would be the joint responsibility of the ' province, the municipalities and the farmers, but the initial cost of $6,750,000 would be the responsibility of the federal government. The completion of this irrigation project would bring about a complete transformation of that area and bring prosperity where there has been want for many years. It will bring prosperity where there has been want for many years, and put that whole area to a very large extent upon a self-supporting basis.
Let us think what the result of the completion of that project would mean. First, there would be a tremendous expansion of production; second, there would be a great expansion of revenue for the government from that production; then, of course, there would be a great increase in the general well-being of the farmers in that whole area; and it would also mean a great reduction in payments of relief to the farmers. So that I do not think we can say we cannot afford that project; it might very well be said that we cannot afford not to carry it out.
In the thirties we used to hear a good deal about the danger of expanding our production and thereby creating a surplus. The tragic period through which we are going at this time should teach us a lesson that we should never forget. Never again, I hope, shall we be guilty of destroying food and allowing our resources to go to waste. One of the greatest resources we have in western Canada is water, which is going to waste day by day. I believe our aim and the aim of every nation should be to maintain a brimming pool of consumer goods; in the first instance, to maintain the well-being of our own people, exchanging our surplus goods for the surplus goods of other nations, and in the event that we can produce more than we need we would be in the enviable position of being able to assist nations less fortunately situate than ourselves, and in that way be making a great contribution

to peace. If the governments of prosperous nations fail to live up to the principles of the Atlantic charter and the Hot Springs food conference, the outlook for peace in the world will be pretty bleak.
I should also like to issue this warning. If in the future as we expand farm production we allow that expansion of production to be an excuse for reducing prices w'e shall very soon find that production will be reduced. Unfortunately that is what has happened in the past. When farmers produced abundantly it caused a reduction in price, with the result that production was discouraged. So that, whatever policy we have in the future, it must be one which will make it possible to maintain maximum production and at the same time a fair price to the producer.
Since under this item we are discussing irrigation, I would urge upon the minister the desirability of bringing about the immediate construction of the various irrigation projects which have been surveyed in western Canada. If the war were still in operation, and these projects were considered necessary to the carrying on of the war, I do not doubt that they would be carried out, almost overnight. Unfortunately, just as soon as peace comes, we seem to suffer a form of creeping paralysis. I should like to ask the minister whether he can give any assurance that actual construction will be started on a number _ of these projects in western Canada at a very early day. When we were discussing this question on April 8, I think it was, the minister stated that' he did not know whether it would be possible to do any actual construction work so far as the larger irrigation schemes were concerned; $750,000 was to be spent on the St. Mary's project, but he did not know whether any actual construction work would be done on the other ones. Could the minister give us any information on that point?

Last year we spent some money on the St, Mary's dam project in the form of making surveys and checking on the engineering which had previously been done. This year we have in these votes $750,000 with which to proceed with construction. Tenders have been called for the construction of part of that work and contracts will be allotted within a few days in connection with it. As far as the Red Deer diversion is concerned, we have already taken from the $10 millions referred to, $115,000 for engineering and surveying during the present season. That has already been asked for and obtained by P.F.R.A. to proceed with that survey work. For the Saskatchewan river project $137,000 has already been obtained, and the survey

Supply-Agriculture
and engineering work in connection with these two projects is proceeding. It is understood, of course, by the hon. member for Acadia that ever since about 1938 we have been doing a certain amount of engineering work on the project. The engineering work which is now being done is the checking of that work by an expert. If he finds any fault with any of the engineering decisions which have been made 'he will indicate that further checks will have to be made in connection with it. If he finds that the engineering is satisfactory and the results which have been recommended are also satisfactory of course we shall proceed from there on the basis of the engineering work which has been done.
That is, with the construction?

Yes. I would hesitate to say that we shall be in a position this summer to call for tenders on the work, but at the moment I would not say that we would not be in a position to do so. That is, I would not say that we shall be, but there is the possibility that we may be able to do so.
There is a good chance of going ahead next year, then?
I think so.

I was very much interested in a remark made by the Minister of Agriculture to the effect that 'he was unable to bring down legislation in connection with doing a lot of this work. He said that he could not bring down these bills and do those things which are supposed to be done, because of the failure of the dominion-provincial conference. As a matter of fact, If I understood him aright, he stated that he has been deprived of certain sources of revenue. I should like to know what sources of revenue the minister has been deprived of. At the present time I do not know of any, and I do not think he should use the failure of the dominion-provincial conference as an excuse for not bringing down bills in respect of this work. He says that some sources of revenue should be taxed. What are the sources which should be taxed? I think he ought to give us a little more information about that and not merely lay the blame on the failure of the dominion-provincial conference. As far as the province from which I come is concerned, we are quite willing to help anybody.
Oh, oh.

Yes! Yes! Yes! That is right. We have been willing to do so, and the fact is right on the record. We
can stand on our own feet. I should like to know what are the sources of taxation of which the government is deprived at this time.
I repeat that I do not know of any.

I do not want to enter a discussion of that question. I am afraid that if we got on to that matter my estimates would never pass. All I can say is, my inference was that at the time of confederation certain responsibilities were placed on the provinces and certain responsibilities were placed on the federal government, and among those placed on the provinces were such things as drainage and diking and all those matters about which we have been talking. I think, when we get to the province of Ontario or any other eastern province, even the provincial government does not assume the responsibility in these matters; by legislation they have placed it on the counties and townships; and the row over the back fence about the ditch across a farm does not become a provincial matter but is a municipal matter.
That is right.

The suggestion is that we should take over some of these works which are now the responsibility of the provinces and conduct the developments from Ottawa. There would, of course, be a limit to the extent to which we could do that. If the provinces do not desire to have certain grants from Ottawa, we might spend that money direct instead of making the grants from Ottawa to the province and having somebody else do, it. Speaking of some of the work we might undertake, such as diking in the maritimes, I can think of projects in Ontario related to black marsh lands-
In Kent county.

-where we have been admiring live stock for some years and where we could grow onions and other things to good advantage. The undertaking, however, is too big for the farmer or the municipality, or, in some cases, for the province itself. It would not be too big for Ontario, because my hon. friend says they can stand on their own feet; but if we undertook such obligations in some other provinces, Ontario would expect us to do the same.
I do not think so.

They probably would. We could undertake this under a bill of the kind suggested. I wish to say that I was not making a criticism of any particular province.

The minister says that he has been deprived of certain sources of taxation.

In order to avoid an argument here in regard to the question, I will put the blame on the federal treasury and say that when I go for money to spend on such activities I have to face what the treasury will say.

The minister cannot say in this House of Commons that he has been deprived of any source of taxation, because the federal government is taxing in every field at the present time. That is the whole point. It is, not a question of being deprived of any source of taxation. The minister cannot get away with that. There may be other reasons but he cannot lay the blame there.
May I ask the hon. member a question?

Sit down for a minute, please. We have assisted in many places in levelling land, and we will dig ditches as soon as there is enough organization at the other end to indicate that the water will be used when we take'it there.

I should like to ask a question with respect to the amount of appropriation for water storage for Moose Jaw and Regina. The minister is aware of our problem there. Moose Jaw is definitely short of water. They have not enough for ordinary purposes. In Regina we have reached the
danger point with respect to the continuance of water from our wells out in the Boggy Creek and the Pilot Butte area. I have not the exact amount that has been spent, but at Moose Jaw something over $600,000 has been spent over a period of years. In the first place, that had to do with pumping water from the Saskatchewan river and running it down an open ditch to the Caron area and pumping water into the sand there. The water is then pumped out and into Moose Jaw by the city itself, a distance of some eighteen miles. On that project we have spent something over $600,000. It is the only place in Canada where the federal government has undertaken to make water available to a city. The only reason that we undertook that was there was a combination of circumstances existing. It was a drought period; it was a period of unemployment prior to the war, and there was the possibility of irrigation along the way, farmers requiring irrigation. Because of that combination of circumstances we said that we would try the experiment of pumping water in an open ditch down to within eighteen miles of Moose Jaw, conditionally upon Moose Jaw pumping the water out of there and into Moose Jaw. The minister referred to the Moose Jaw water supply, and it is in that respect I wish to speak particularly for a few minutes.
