I take the same stand as is taken by the bureau of reclamation in the United States. We must remember that it could be said that, because of permission being given to the Canadian Pacific railway to have its divisional works at Moose Jaw, without first making certain that there would be an ample water supply for the engines of that railway, which has done so much to open up western Canada, the government is responsible for the fact that a town has grown up where the railway first built its shops in that part of the country. To that extent the country is responsible for the city's development at a point on the prairies where there is insufficient water supply to permit its full growth.
I have said before, and I repeat, that whatever is decided by the government in the matter of spending money to bring a water supply from the Saskatchewan river, the only permanent and abundant available supply for both Moose Jaw and Regina, will have my undivided support. As a businessman I know, from my past experience in big business in Canada, that an increase in the population of those two cities to three or four times their present size would be beneficial to all Canada. And they cannot help all Canada as they would do unless they are amply supplied with water.
I shall not repeat what has been said by others and what I have said on other occasions, but I shall close this part of my remarks by saying that I will support any government programme designed to provide an abundant and permanent water supply for 63260-128
those two cities. I look forward anxiously to learning what is contained in the report the minister will receive from the engineers now engaged in drilling holes up and down the river, north and south of Riverhurst. I am firmly convinced that the Supreme Being, in His wisdom, when permitting those cities to be located there, had made ample provision somewhere in that river, and that the source will eventually be found.
I would point out to the committee briefly that we should not be critical of expenditures in connection with this vote. The engineers engaged by the department, through the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, are compelled to spend considerable sums of money without showing much, if any return. That is not their fault. I know something about that kind of engineering, and I know they can drill many holes in the river without showing any satisfactory results. But holes have to be drilled to find a safe bottom upon which to build a dam-if, indeed, it is possible to find a safe bottom. If they did not, then they would have to build a dam which would be much more expensive than the one required if a safe bottom were found.
I hold in my hand the core of a diamond drill. This one came from the St. Mary's river, at which point, I understood the minister to say this afternoon, contracts are to be let shortly for the St. Mary's river dam. I should imagine the purpose would be, first, to divert the river, and then to proceed with the building of a dam. It would seem that on that river they have found a safe and sure bottom, of which this is a core. I am happy that the St. Mary's river work is proceeding satisfactorily.
I listened to what the minister had to say about the Red Deer work. There, too, I might say, they have found a safe bottom on the Red Deer river. If I were to break this core in two, I am sure hon. members would not know whether one-half was from the Red Deer or from the St. Mary's. I know now that the department has found a safe bottom on the Red Deer river, about which the hon. member for Acadia spoke this afternoon.
I was most happy in February last to meet the hon. member in the really smart town of Hanna, a town which some day will be a city, if the programme the department has

The United States bureau of reclamation is spending $160,000,000 this year in carrying on a gigantic programme. By 1951 they will have reclaimed 6,500,000 acres of land just as dry and the same type of land as that which lies between Buffalo Lake and Hanna and in the southern part of Alberta where the hon. member for Lethbridge comes from. Some of that land around Lethbridge now looks like the garden of Eden because of the irrigation projects they have there. The improvement will be much greater when other projects are completed, but I am not going to discuss them at the moment.
I understand that the first irrigation project in America Was carried on by some friends of the hon. member for Lethbridge at Salt Lake City. . When those pioneers went from Illinois to the west and started to build that magnificent temple which is one of the finest buildings in the world they found the ground so dry that they could not pick it. They brought water from the lake in order to make the ground soft enough to work and they conceived the idea of irrigation. Later they brought those

ideas up to Alberta. Those pioneer settlers deserve a lot of credit for what they did in Alberta.
The bureau of reclamation states in its latest report that the average net return from irrigated farms under their jurisdiction is $36.33 per acre. Throughout the whole United States, including those prolific states of Iowa and Kansas, the average is only $14.41 per acre. When irrigation gives such wonderful results how can any one say that it is not self-liquidating.
I hope the minister will not hesitate to bring in whatever programme is required to irrigate these lands which my hon. friend spoke of this afternoon. We should have a programme to irrigate the semi-dry acres of our western prairie land which now grows nothing but sage; wild rose and prairie grass. I presume that if I wanted to buy some of that land to-day I would not have to pay more than $2.50 or $5 per acre. But, once it is irrigated, the land would be worth anything up to $50 per acre. If special crops were grown it could easily be worth $75 to $100 per acre. The difference in land value alone would pay for the cost of irrigating, and that is apart al- ' together from the magnificent crop returns which would be obtained.
I do not care what government brings in a programme to irrigate the Hanna and Acadia and Buffalo Lake areas, it will get my support. I think the minister knows that the land from Buffalo Lake south has a slope which would permit a flow of water. The more I examine our whole western country, the more I am convinced that God Almighty has laid it out in such a way, with the great river behind it, that it is possible to have a flow downhill. Very little pumping, such as they have to do in the United States and which they find it pays them to do, would have to be done in the Buffalo Lake to Hanna area.

For the benefit of some members of the house who at one time or another have seemed to show a lack of appreciation of the difficulties which face a large part of the farming population of the west, may I be permitted to make a few comments? Almost every year some part of the west has a partial or a complete crop failure because of the vagaries of the weather or because of the ravages of plant disease, as in the case of cereal
rust and too from insect pests, which frequently cause a total loss of crop. This brings about a wide fluctuation in farm income and, in many instances, creates real distress and hardship. I come from that district and I doubt if anyone else here has spent as long a time as I have in the particular area affected. I have witnessed that hardship on many occasions in the more than forty years that I have lived in southern Saskatchewan where the crop has failed because of want of rain, and dire poverty has resulted because the crops have never reached maturity. The Prairie Farm Assistance Act was enacted primarily for the purpose of relieving such distressful conditions in the areas affected, and has, I may say, been a definite improvement over the old system of relief which was in vogue during the thirties.
I wish to commend the government on this move, because I feel it is certainly a step in the right direction; it is progressive. But at this time I desire to draw the minister's attention to certain dissatisfactions which seem to prevail, at least in some quarters of the west, with regard to the administration of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. I hope that the minister will accept what I have to say in the spirit in which it is given. While there is criticism of the administration, I shall endeavour to be fair and offer constructive suggestions which I hope will be given careful consideration by the government.
In the first place, before the act becomes operative the federal government must declare a crop failure region or an emergency year. This is done at the discretion of the federal authorities, and only when 171 townships are involved in crop failure. Many farmers are of the opinion that the act should apply automatically whenever an applicant, through the loss of his crop, and through no fault of his own, is in need of assistance. Furthermore, ,1 should like to suggest to the minister that, since revision is under consideration, some thought be given to the young veterans and others under twenty-one years of age who are still residing with their parents and operating farms elsewhere because they have been unable as yet to set up homes for themselves. I suggest that if at eighteen years of age they are eligible and old enough to fight for the country they should be eligible, even though they are under twenty-one, to receive benefits under Prairie Farm Assistance Act.

That the crop failure bonus be increased to $5 per acre, and that the maximum be $1,000 and the assessment two per cent, and that payments be made on an individual basis.

So far as the operating of this act is concerned, I believe that the wider possibilities of a crop insurance plan should be carefully explored by the government. The minister may reply to this suggestion that such a scheme would be feasible only under the jurisdiction of the provinces. But it appears to me there should be no objection by the federal Department of Agriculture to at least exploring the possibilities of a nation-wide crop insurance plan, even though the implementing of the scheme by federal authorities may be ultra vires at the moment.
If the plan is then considered practicable, arrangements could be made to subsidize the provinces, or better still to have an amendment to the British North America Act introduced to take care of the situation, as was necessary for unemploment insurance, to give the federal government jurisdiction in the field.
In order to have stability in farm income some comprehensive system of crop insurance appears vital. It is generally recognized that such a scheme would require substantial contributions from the federal treasury. I submit that even though that may be necessary it would be a wiser policy than to leave the farmers in the unhappy state of having to accept relief when a series of crop failures occur.
The farmers' levy to the fund would still have to be based on production, and of necessity would vary from year to year, as do the contributions of the industrial worker to the unemployment insurance fund. Crops have

long been insured against hail damage. There seems to be no adequate reason why crops should not be insured against damage from frost, drought, insects or ravages of plant disease in the very same way. The fruit grower who suffers a loss of crop because the fruit blossoms are destroyed by a late spring frost and the truck farmer who suffers because of insects destroying his vegetables need protection quite as much as do the cereal farmers. Any plan of crop insurance therefore should include fruit, tobacco and vegetable crops, as well as cereals. I noticed that the Minister of Agriculture, in replying to a suggestion the other night that a crop insurance scheme rather than a scheme of assistance in time of crop failure should be brought in, stated that all studies as to the feasibility of a strictly crop insurance scheme had shown that such a scheme was not feasible in that part of Canada at least.
The reason it is not feasible is that the area is large, and has a variable yield. Investments farmers have to make are high. More than that, the farmer receives for his products prices which vary widely. Any scheme of crop insurance practised in the past has collected an almost uniform rate from the farmer, based upon the sales he makes. The payments made out are on a fixed basis. For that reason, whenever prices go down, the crop insurance scheme goes bankrupt.
While I should be very glad to see Manitoba given a chance to withdraw from the operation of the act, if they so wish, I would suggest that if in future years we have poor prices for our farm products, a crop insurance scheme will not be able to work, even in Manitoba, and that the people in that province will be wanting to get back under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act very quickly. When we are discussing any crop insurance scheme we should keep in mind the fact that in the past the government has had to come to the assistance of farming communities in a way that is far less desirable than under the present Prairie Farm Assistance Act. Between 1930 and 1939, governments in Canada spent in Saskatchewan alone $156 million on relief. In that province in the last six years the Prairie Farm Assistance Act has cost the federal treasury about $20 million. The act cost the federal government in the year in which Saskatchewan had its poorest crop yield since the act was in operation, the sum of $11 million. But in 1937 the government paid $47 million in relief to take care of the people in that province in the absence of a proper scheme of crop failure assistance.
A number of crop insurance schemes have been tried in various countries of the world, and particularly some extensive operations in the United States. In every case, every crop insurance plan undertaken has failed miserably. In order that a proper insurance scheme may be feasible at all it must operate in an area in which yields vary little. For instance, in the crop insurance scheme used in the United States in a county in Ohio, where the yield was 21-7 bushels per acre on a long-time average, and where the crops were insured for half of that amount, the farmer to insure a crop of at least eleven bushels to the acre had

to pay only two per cent of his annual sales. In the county of Morton, Kansas, where the average yield was only 7-7 bushels per acre, to get insurance of something less than four bushels per acre the farmer had to pay each year 26-3 per cent of his sales as a premium.
So it is obvious that in any area in which there is a great variation, the premiums which must be collected to cover even a meagre scheme of crop insurance are very high, and the farmers naturally think they cannot afford that type of crop insurance. Consequently they withdraw from the plan; and those farmers who have crops almost every year- and good crops-stay under the scheme because they can probably get an insurance rate of around two per cent.

That is, I think, a strong argument for putting the administration of the act on an individual farmer basis.

I do not know if any part of Saskatchewan is susceptible to flood damage, but there are certain areas in Manitoba, including the constituency of Provencher, where flood damage is somewhat more serious than drought or hail damage, and if the act could be so amended that compensation could be paid in the case of flood and hail as well as drought in Manitoba I am sure that the farmers of that province would not advocate withdrawing from the act.

Before the discussion goes any further I should like to say something which I had intended to say at an earlier stage. I want to express my own appreciation to the hon. member for Wood Mountain for having given to this committee the very careful outline that he has of some of the shortcomings of what we sometimes call crop insurance. I take from his remarks that he has made a very careful study of it, and I judge from what he said that he was much in favour of crop failure assistance rather than crop insurance. While I was listening to what, he had to say, I thought it would be well worth while for hon. members who have been discussing these two ideas, the one of crop failure assistance and the other of crop insurance, to take the trouble to read that part of his speech w'hich deals with that matter. It. bears out fully, I think, what has been contended by myself, as the originator of this-
Supply-Agriculture

idea, from the beginning, that in an area such as Saskatchewan, particularly crop insurance as such is almost impossible, for the reasons which were given; and the illustration mentioned as between a state in the United States wftere they seldom have crop failure and another state where they have it quite regularly is the best indication of what happens to those who rely upon insurance as against crop failure assistance in areas of that kind.
Other matters which were brought up cover most of the objections to the act. One thing I have been urging, and urging rather strongly recently, was given the greatest emphasis by two of the speakers, namely that the situation is probably not quite the same since young men started to come back from overseas as it was before they went overseas. The provision which is in the regulation-it is not in the act -to the effect that a young man under the age of twenty who lived with his parents was not paid, had not much more to do with the claims than simply this, th'at there was an effort, when the act was first brought in, by a very limited number of people to collect more money under the act than they were really entitled to. A man with, let us say, two or three sections of land was entitled to collect only on half of 400 acres, or 200, but by dividing that land among a certain number of members of his family he could get all the land under the compensation provisions. Some of the regulations were inserted in order to avoid that, and one of the methods of simplifying the administration which was strongly recommended for a considerable time before it was brought in was that the age limit be put in. That may have been all right at the time and it did not create much difficulty until this year, but men have been coming back from overseas since last year who could not possibly have been utilizing any method of that kind in order to obtain greater advantages under the act. I have been suggesting for some time that that regulation ought to be changed and perhaps made to apply retroactively, but at the moment I am not able to say that it will be. It has to be given further consideration and brought in for change. I can see, however, that there is some reason for that.
When the act gets before the committee, hon. members who are interested in that area will be able to discuss the question, and there is no member who has greater reason to be interested in the area than the hon. member for Wood Mountain. The area has been under drought for a considerable number of years. I think it will be agreed when we go over the act carefully and make some changes in

the regulations as they now stand, that most of the restrictions which are there must exist for the general reason that restrictions of this kind are put into legislation, namely, to safeguard the treasury, which, after all, represents the money of the people against a few who sometimes take advantage of conditions, and unfortunately there are people who suffer in consequence. It is not easy to overcome some of the difficulties that exist by any method other than the regulations that are here, but these matters can remain for discussion until the act is before the committee.

I do not wish to take up any time repeating what has already been said, but I desire to bring to the attention of the minister a specific instance that has been brought to his notice previously in the course of correspondence. I have also taken it up a number of times with the officials of his department who have given me a most courteous hearing but who invariably have-advised me of the impossibility of doing anything toward relieving the situation.
The hon. member for Souris, who has given profound study to the matter, both since being in the house and prior to that time in connection with his position as president of the municipalities' association of Manitoba, has pressed for a long time, together with other members, for payment on an individual basis. I realize the difficulties in the way of that being carried into effect, but it does seem unfair that many are denied the payment of the bonus by reason of the regulations or because they do not live in an area sufficiently large to bring them within the regulations. They are required to make a contribution, in return for which they get nothing, unless the area that suffers drought damage is large enough. I refer particularly to an area north of Regina in the rural municipality of Dufferin. That area is bordered on the south by a water course. Across that water course the crops are invariably good, while north of the water course they are invariably bad; but because the area is less than one-quarter of a township, they are unable to secure payment of any bonus whatsoever. They have been in that position for the last several years.
They live at the top of the valley.

The minister knows the area. They live right at the top of the valley; they pay year by year, and they suffer loss year by year. It is all very well to ask, why do they not get out? They cannot get out. The fact remains that each year they sow, and it so happens that for the past

four or five years, and even prior to that, they have suffered losses and have never had any return.
I fully realize that legislation, however carefully drafted it may be, cannot cover every eventuality. But there is an area that has suffered repeated failures, and there are two other similar areas in other parts of the province. I suggest that, when amendments are brought down, something be done to cover that situation.
With regard to the matter raised by the hon. member for Wood Mountain, in what all must have regarded as a most able and constructive address, he mentioned the case of some man who was not living on the farm and *was denied payment of the bonus. I realize that there, too, there are difficulties in the way; but I feel that section 5, subsection 6, which gives the minister power to make regulations excluding from the operation of this act farmers who do not reside upon farms within the meaning of the regulation, should be reviewed and changes should be made in connection therewith.
Let me mention one example. An elderly couple have lived on the farm until they find it necessary to leave and have someone work the farm. I might mention also cases such as the hon. member for Wood Mountain pointed out of individuals who go into town to earn a living temporarily. I suggest that when an opportunity is given to discuss this matter in the committee on agriculture, and when the amendments are brought down, questions such as have been referred to this evening should receive the consideration of the draftsman to the end that the anomalies which now exist be removed. I do not like repetition, but I again urge the minister to do something with respect to the area I mentioned near Bethune, Saskatchewan, and two or three others, with a view to having these people, who are bona fide farmers and who have struggled against adversity for years, be given consideration such as this act is designed to afford. I suggest that something be done to meet the situation of farmers who, by reason of drought, have not a reasonable crop.

Another problem has given trouble in the past and I do not know whether provision has been made to meet it. I refer to the farmer who has one, two or more sons working on the farm with him. They may all
have their own separate crops, but because they all use the same set of machinery they have been given only one bonus..

That is not the intention. The regulations do not prevent a son from living with his parents and using the same equipment as his parents use. As a matter of fact, the intention was that they should be encouraged to do this rather than discouraged. But there are cases where that is given as the reason-though other reasons develop -why they are not allowed the payment. It may be that the board have decided that the arrangement is not a bona fide one.

Can the minister explain the formula used for deciding whether a man is a farmer or a rancher? Two or three years ago the minister himself criticized strongly some of the decisions that have been handed down, and recently I have run into a good deal of trouble regarding a number of men who were termed ranchers but who, in my opinion, were farmers. In the area south of the Goose Lake line it takes an average of forty acres to one head of cattle. So that if a man had seventy-five head of cattle he would have to have 3,000 acres for pasture; and if he farmed 200 acres it would be decided that, having 3,000 acres for pasture and 200 acres for crops, he must be a rancher. In such circumstances a man could be a farmer, although he had 3,000 acres for pasture land.

I understand that
shortly after the matter was discussed in the house on a previous occasion-as a matter of fact, I had some discussion with the board -the board was changed and a new chairman put on it. These matters were all discussed fully, and I understand that that interpretation has not been put on the ranchers since.
How do you arrive at what is a rancher; what is the formula?

As a matter of fact, I insisted that there should be no arriving at it at all; that anybody who did not know what a rancher was in western Canada should not be on that board. I told them that I would try to see that he was not on unless he was able to determine what was a rancher himself, without any definition being put down. Anyone out there knows what a rancher is.
I did not have any trouble for about two years and then within the past month or two I have received a number of letters protesting about it. I think I had better hand them over to Mr. Stevenson.

Send them over and I shall have a look at them. I might say that I was getting a lot of complaints before I

took action. I think none have come to me since that time. I hope the board is not getting back to its old practice.

That is one of the amendments proposed. I cannot say it will get here, but I hope it will.

Since I have the honour to represent perhaps one of the largest producers of cheese in the Dominion of Canada I feel that a large percentage of this money will eventually come back to my constituency, because I am quite sure that the cheese-makers there can be favourably compared with those of any other part of Canada.
For the information of the committee, I may say that last year in Oxford county we produced some eight million pounds of cheese. That is a lot of cheese. I should also like to bring a matter to the attention of the minister to show him that in Oxford county we treasure the dairy cow. I believe we are the only county in Canada which has erected a statue to the memory of a dairy cow after she has passed to her great

reward. I refer to that wonderful cow Spring-bank Snow Countess, owned, bred and milked by Mr. Tom Dent of the city of Woodstock. Mr. Dent is now a member of the Ontario legislature at Toronto.
A Progressive Conservative?
Yes, he is a Conservative.
Don't blame that on the cow.

On the outskirts of the city of Woodstock on the very ground where this cow used to graze, eat the grass to produce this wonderful record of 9,300 pounds of but-terfat in her lifetime lactation period, stands a mohument or statue, life-sized, with floodlights on it at night. Things are going along not too badly in the dairy industry in Oxford apart from a little dispute over prices, but there is another matter that I should like to bring to the attention of the minister at this time. Mr. Chairman, I may be entirely out of order, but if I am no doubt you will correct me.- This matter should have really come up under the diseases of animals item, but I was unavoidably absent on that occasion. When that item was under discussion I understand no hon. member mentioned mastitis, a dread disease which is making serious inroads into the production of milk in western Ontario at the present time. I know of a complete herd which has gone to the butcher's block because of it. Mastitis is a very contagious infection. It gets into the udder of the cow, and when the dairy cow loses her udder she has lost everything. Have the federal government taken any steps to combat this disease, or are they making any studies of it? I wish the minister would answer that question. I have been approached by many farmers of my riding and they certainly are concerned over this matter. I have many farmers in my riding with 200 acre farms; it is not uncommon for them to produce up to 2,500 pounds of milk a day, and that requires a lot of milking. When this disease gets in the herd I know for a fact that their production has been halved. There are certain remedies that I know veter-

inarians have been using, but I believe that further study should be made into this important matter.	[DOT]

As the hon. member said, the item was up some days ago, but the disease of mastitis was not mentioned in the discussion that took place. We spent most of our time on Bang's disease. For a number of years studies have been under way that finally resulted in the.discovery of a method which appears to give most promising results. Penicillin used under conditions which ensure an accurate diagnosis has proved capable of curing approximately 90 per cent of the infected quarter. Every effort is being made to encourage the use of this drug under conditions which aim at total elimination of the disease from the herd. It is believed that only when this is put into practice will the economic burden caused by this disease be removed. Therefore the investigations have been made. I have been sitting here now for some weeks listening attentively to the interesting discussion in connection with the Department of Agriculture. I have listened to hon. members from the west pleading for assistance for their people, because it is too dry. I have listened to hon. members from the east pleading that it is too wet. I happen to live in between, less than a hundred miles from Ottawa, and I would not want anyone to have the impression that we are either too dry or too wet. But we do, at times, really suffer from drought, and sometimes from too much rain. However, we are fortunate in being able to crawl up on the high spots when it is too wet, and when it is dry we go down to the lower places.
So far as assistance is concerned, in my particular part of the country I think the minister will agree that it must come particularly from this item. I should like some explanation of the subsidy for the construction and reconstruction of cheese factories. Mine is a dairying part of the country, and I was not of the opinion that cheese factory construction received much assistance. I do not know in what way that assistance is given.
In fact, we have lost a number of cheese factories to milk factories. Would the minister be good enough to. break down the item? I am not referring, to equipment, but rather to the reconstruction of cheese factories. The amount is increased this year from $50,000 to $250,000, which would look as though we might expect something further by way of building and maintenance of cheese factories.

The vote has been in existence since 1939, and was put into effect for the purpose of improving the quality of cheese. There were two ways taken, as was suggested a few minutes ago, to bring about that improvement; one was to pay for high-quality cheese the amount of one cent on 93 score and two cents on 94 score. In addition to that, provision was made for spending money to improve equipment; that is, to get refrigeration into the curing room, and to . improve curing rooms in order to assist in improving the standard of cheese.
In addition to that, in quite a number of places there were factories which were very much out of date. Then, in some places there were more factories in those districts than were required. They were not able to make things go. Too many of them had been established, and we wanted to encourage them perhaps to do away with one and to improve the other. We agreed. to do certain things to assist along those lines.
Those were summed up in this way: (a) to encourage the consolidation of existing factories in order to secure improvement and greater uniformity of quality of production through increased production per factory;
(b)	to assist in providing improved cheese maturing facilities in cheese factories which will result in improved quality and reduce loss of weight during maturing;
(c)	to assist in a standardization of diameter of cheese pressing equipment, thereby securing improved appearance of the cheese. That is, many of the old presses were of different sizes. Some of them built a high cheese instead of a flat cheese. To get it standardized, we gave assistance to have that equipment changed.
(d)	to provide for the payment of a premium for highest quality cheese. I gave the premiums when I spoke a few minutes ago.
Then, it has been pointed out that the item this year is $250,000 as against $50,000 last year. The point is that last year we were unable to get the materials. During the war, as hon. members know, many of the materials required for doing these things were not available. It was anticipated more of them would be available this year, and we would be able to overtake many of the applications that are in. That is, for subsidies for construction and reconstruction of cheese factories, the improvement of cheese maturing facilities in cheese factories, and for the standardization of cheese pressing equipment. We expect to be able to get five times as much equipment as we got last year. We could have
Supply-Agriculture

spent the amount last year if we had been able to get the equipment. But we were not able to get it.

I understand this large item of $1,750,000 for premiums on high quality cheese. But the item which was not quite clear to me was the one for $250,000. Have any subsidies been paid for construction and maintenance of cheese factories in the county of Leeds?

I am not sure that we have the information for counties, but we have it for provinces. Under the item of amalgamation, we have amalgamated 47 in Quebec, three in Ontario. In the matter of insulation, there have been 150 in Quebec,
19 in Ontario, two in Manitoba and one in Alberta. For insulation and refrigeration there have been 242 in Quebec, 262 in Ontario, seven in Alberta and one in British Columbia. For pressing equipment there have been eight in New Brunswick, four in Prince Edward Island, two in Quebec, 141 in Ontario, and one in British Columbia.
The totals for all are: New Brunswick, eight; Prince Edward Island, 4; Quebec, 441; Ontario, 425; Manitoba, two; Alberta, eight, and British Columbia, two.
While I have not the information by counties, I am reasonably sure that there has been some reequipment in the county of Leeds, and that they have received payments under the provision for reequipment. Perhaps they have not received anything in respect ' of the rebuilding of factories.

In the last month or six weeks the minister has referred frequently to a procedure in Quebec whereby factories have become convertible into cheese factories or butter factories, as opportunity for sale of one or other of these commodities seems to become more attractive. Has any part of this $250,000 been devoted to effecting this convertibility in respect of the butter and cheese factories in Quebec?

I would doubt very much if any considerable proportion of it has been used for that purpose. There may have been instances where it has been proposed to add a cheese factory to a building already producing butter, in which event they would probably come under the regulations as applied to equipment. But that is a condition which, as I understand it, has existed in Quebec for many years. They have had duplex plants, I do not know what their origin was, or who originally advocated their operation. But the fact is that they have those duplex plants and, strange to say,

there are very few of them anywhere but Quebec. One may wonder why that should be so, but the fact remains. Someone must have promoted the idea at one time, and succeeded in having a considerable number of them established in that province.

Has the minister any detailed information on this particular phase of the enterprise? He made several references to it. The fact that I am not thoroughly familiar with the situation is of no great significance, but I must point out that I have not been able to localize many of those factories, nor have I been able to find many instances where a change from cheese making to butter making has taken place.

I had the figures here the other night when we were discussing it, but I do not know whether I can locate them at the moment. Would the hon. member mind if I got the information for him and give it to him to-morrow in typewritten form?
That is quite satisfactory.

Cheese production this year is down considerably as compared with the same period last year. If my figures are correct it is down 35-8 per cent for the four months. The estimates provide for $1,750,000 for quality cheese, which is the same as was voted last year. In many instances the subsidy is not forthcoming to the cheese factories in the late fall and the patrons do not receive it for some time. Some cheese factories borrow the money and pay the subsidies and then wait until it is passed by the government for the ensuing year. Beginning June 1, cheese is being requisitioned for the British market. After that date all cheese manufactured in Ontario and Quebec will have to be sent to the dairy products board for shipment to the United Kingdom.
Does the minister think that, with the prices now prevailing for milk going into cheese, he will be able to supply the 125,000,000 pounds which wre have contracted to ship to the United Kingdom this year? If he does not, then I suggest that some arrangement be made whereby, if all this $250,000 for the improvement of cheese factories and equipment is not required this year, an extra premium for quality be paid to producers. I believe the minister is on the right track in paying a subsidy for quality, because I think the records will show that since this subsidy was put on there has been a great improvement in the quality of cheese manufactured in this country. If the minister does not think he is going to get this 125,000,000 pounds of

Supply-Agriculture
cheese for the United Kingdom, when he brings down his supplementary estimates he should give further consideration to increasing the quality premium.

I do not want to discourage anyone, but our officials do not expect to get the 125,000,000 pounds, of cheese for export this year, no matter what we do. Our feed position seems to be such as not to permit of that being accomplished. The only thing that may make it possible is particularly good grass during the summer. We are requisitioning all cheese after June 1 to go to the United Kingdom, but we are not requisitioning cheese in May. Some think that the figure we shall reach will be 115,000,0000 pounds and others think that we shall not reach even that. I took the position that we should not lower our sights, that we should aim at 125,000,000 pounds. This matter has been discussed with the British and they understand the position. They do not anticipate getting 125,000,000 pounds, but if we produce it they want it; they want even more than that if we can produce it.
Then, as to whether we shall make use of the $250,000, if we can get the equipment there will be no difficulty about using that vote, or perhaps even more. There is enough demand to use that up and perhaps we can get the equipment. We have voted $1,750,000 for premium subsidies, but I should not like to say that our estimates at the moment show that we shall reach that point.
The hon. member suggests that we should pay more. It is purely a question of whether we can maintain it, not only this year but at other times. It is most difficult to take off these premiums once you put them on. This premium has done very well up to date, as has been suggested. There is another danger to be faced. If you get it up too high, somebody takes it all off. Up to date we have been able to maintain it. Every time the estimates are under consideration before they come here the question is raised whether we should not take it off. It has been maintained at its present level and we have been able to indicate good results. I would hesitate to add another cent this year and then have somebody take it all off next year or the year after.

In his remarks the other day on another item the minister suggested that prices paid in Canada were about the same as prevailing prices in the United States. I asked him if it was not a fact that most of the cheese manufactured in the United States was manufactured from skim milk, and I think he more or less agreed -with me. I think the minister
was making a comparison which was not fair to the farmers of this country. If cheese in the United States is manufactured from skim milk the farmer there has a benefit of three or four pounds of butter fat for every 100 pounds of milk he produces. Consequently the return to the farmer in the United States would be considerably aboye the return to the farmer in Canada. Will the minister make it clear whether cheese in the United States is produced mostly from skim milk?

Wisconsin cheese, to which I was referring the other night, is a Cheddar cheese similar to our own. If you were to go to the United States and take cheese at different points you would get different results. The prices I gave the other day were the prices that had obtained. I became a little concerned about them myself, and I asked the officials to get me not only the prices but the subsidies that are paid on both sides of the line. Figured out on the basis of the return in Wisconsin on milk that goes into cheese, the return to the farmer is much higher than it is in Canada.
When you consider the subsidies which have been increased1 recently in order to get more cheese on to the market to be shipped to Europe and elsewhere, the total return from milk going into cheese in Wisconsin would be $3.03 per hundred. In Ontario, if you take a similar kind of cheese, it is $2.10, or a difference of 93 cents.
In Quebec it is much lower.
It is lower by the amount of the subsidy.

I am fully aware that it is important to produce a high grade of cheese and almost equally important to have good buildings and good equipment. Would the minister briefly outline the procedure in making application for assistance in buildings and equipment and state the percentage of subsidy in both cases?

The act provides in the case of cold storage equipment that 50 per cent will be paid by the government and 50 per cent by the individual. The same provision is made with regard to buildings. We pay 50 per cent where it has been agreed that the improvement will be brought about. The procedure followed in making application is that the person or company writes in and we send out an inspector who inspects the plant and determines whether the improvement can be made and whether we would be warranted in spending the money necessary

to have it made. After the inspection, the application is passed by my office and then goes to council and goes through practically as an order in council.
Would a butter factory becoming a cheese factory be an improvement within the interpretation of the item?
I doubt very much if that happens. It possibly could happen indirectly through a person making application for assistance and putting up a new plant which replaces the creamery.
I suppose the converse would not apply in any event.
Are these outright grants to individual butter plants or cheese factories?
Yes.

eligible for these grants?

The item was $300,000 some years ago and now it is $200,000. In 1937 or 1938 the Americans were objecting to our maple syrup being shipped to the United States because it contained lead, and it was condemned as having lead poisoning in it. They would only permit our maple syrup to be used at that time for the purpose of sweetening cigarettes, and that applied to some of the syrup produced across the line. Upon investigation, we found that lead got into the syrup through the lead covering on the cans put out to catch the syrup and through the lead covering on the vats. They are covered with lead to prevent rusting. I am speaking from memory, because it was quite a few years back. The lead got into the sap, in that way and finally into the syrup. We undertook to assist in improving the equipment on a three-way plan, the individual bearing one-third, the provincial government one-third, and the dominion one-third, of the cost of changing that equipment. The plan went along and we spent about $300,000 in one or two years before the war, but when the war started it was difficult to get the equipment, and the amount spent was very much lower. programme. We have an item of $200,000 this year. If we are able to procure more equipment we shall come along with a supplementary, because we want to have this - change made as rapidly as possible. This item is to pay our share of the cost of changing over to the new equipment.

37.	Agricultural research special projects,
Just what projects are being carried on under this appropriation?

The main one is carrying on experiments at Portage la Prairie in connection with flax. There is another research project being carried on at Lethbridge in connection with wool, and one at Morden which is being carried on more particularly in connection with fruits. These are not the type of project which I myself had in mind or. I think, which the committee had in mind when this appropriation was recommended some three years ago. The equipment was not available with which to equip a plant of that kind, and it was difficult to get building material. This year it has been suggested to me that we take on a half dozen of these special projects again, and I to-day returned the suggestion to the director of experimental farms and asked him to reconsider it. I think the money ought to be spent just as soon as it possibly can be spent to establish a much more effective plant somewhere in western Canada which would do somewhat the same service for the west as much of our research work at the central experimental farm here is doing for the eastern part of Canada. I hope we shall be able to get started on it this year. If not, we shall utilize the money to go on with the investigations at a number of points.
The reason I asked was that I wondered 'whether the work was to be carried on at Saskatoon, where, I believe, the national research council are constructing a laboratory.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce had a vote for that. It is not covered under this vote.

It is the same amount, and I wondered if it was the same vote, or if you people were going to work in conjunction with them. It might not be a bad idea, because probably it could be done more' economically in one place rather than by erecting separate buildings

I understand that the other project is likely to be carried out at Saskatoon. I think that is the understanding of all three provinces. That is one reason why we have been waiting; we do not want to proceed with this until we know what will be done in that respect.
Item agreed to.

speechtext: 200. Departmental administration, $422,774.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
It is the custom, I believe, to make some remarks of an introductory nature on the first item of a department's estimates. I promise that these general remarks of mine will be brief and, I trust, to the point.
Of the importance of the work of this department in the two fields of health and welfare there can be no question whatever. Actually there is not much time spent in this chamber in discussing health and welfare, but I take it as a matter of common ground on the part of us all that these are matters of the highest importance to all Canadians.
I should like to indicate in just a word what will be the attitude of the official opposition with respect to the estimates of this important department. We find, in the first place, that there is a substantial increase in the estimates submitted to us for 1946-47 in comparison with those of the previous year. The increase is largely accounted for by the fact that family allowances will this year be paid on the full twelve-months basis instead of the nine-months basis which prevailed in the previous year. But actually we find proposed in these estimates an increase in the expenditure of the Department of Health and Welfare from a total of $242,372,257.27 in the previous year to a figure of $305,064,716. I am including the items which will be found on page 72 of the main estimates. It will be seen that there is an increase totalling $62,692,458.73 this year as compared with the estimates of last year.
The attitude of the official opposition with respect to these estimates is simply this. Appreciating as we do the tremendous importance of health and welfare, we nevertheless will expect justification for each appropriation sought. It will be our duty in scrutinizing these estimates to see that the taxpayer receives value for the money that he is being called upon to pay, a fair dollar's return to the people of this country in health and welfare for each dollar collected in taxes.
It is a matter of regret-and perhaps I am being rather brash in undertaking to criticize the form of the estimates-that we do not
Supply-Health and Welfare

have before us the actual expenditure in the previous fiscal year. We are given simply two columns: first, the appropriation for the previous year; then, the estimate for the year before us. We are not given the figure of actual expenditure. Compare that with business practice, Mr. Chairman. I do not suppose there is any business which would attempt to set up a budget of estimated expenditure for the current year without having before it the actual expenditure for the previous year, not simply the budget of the previous year, the estimate of expenditure, but the actual expenditure. It is no greater criticism of the form of estimates of this department than of any other that we are not given that information. That is definitely a shortcoming in the form in which estimates are submitted to parliament.
There is another factor which I think hampers the effectiveness of the work of the House of Commons in relation to the estimates. We are not furnished with the report of the department in question for the immediately preceding fiscal year. The last report of the Department of Public Health and Welfare which is issued is the report for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1945. We have no information concerning the detailed operations of the department for the past fourteen months. There will be found in certain of the statutes provision that some of the items which appear in the annual report of the Department of National Health and Welfare must be submitted within three months of the conclusion of the fiscal year. This means that some of these items must be laid before parliament in the form of a report not later than June 30, but, reaching these items as we do on May 30, we are labouring under the handicap of not having that report for the immediately preceding fiscal year.
I make no apology whatever for returning to a theme on which I have spoken once or twice in this house. I dealt with it when we were on the estimates of this department in the fall session. I think we are surely finding day by day the need of a standing committee of this house on health, welfare and social security, and with it I would include housing, because, to my way of thinking, housing must be regarded as inseparably related to the problem of health in this country. We have, of course, an informal committee of the two houses at the present time. It has existed for a number of years; it has no official standing; it is doing good work; but I am satisfied that a standing committee with some official status could do better work. If we had such a committee, I suggest that the study of the estimates would furnish it with an opportunity

of making an effective contribution, both to a careful, systematic scrutiny of the estimates of the department, and to saving this House of Commons valuable time.
A good deal of time spent in consideration of estimates is devoted to obtaining information from the minister as to a multitude of details in relation to the administration of his department, information which, it seems to me, could just as well be obtained in committee. It would then be a matter of record. Those members who wanted information could always find it there and much valuable time would be saved. That is one great service which a standing committee could render in this field.
I think it is patent as well that such a committee would be helpful to parliament in analysing a great many proposals that are put before individual members in the field of social security. I expect that everyone of us receives from time to time ideas. of different individuals as to schemes of social security, and it would be most helpful if there were a standing committee which could review such proposals and make a constructive study of them. I think also of the valuable contributions in the form of proposals put forward from time to time by labour organizations in this country. I take it we are all conscious of the obligation that we owe, both as parliament and as citizens, to labour organizations for the thought and study which organized labour has devoted to problems in the field of national health and welfare. There is no class in the community which has given more constructive thought to problems of national health and welfare than has organized labour in Canada. We do not do justice to these proposals at the present time, nor shall we do justice to them until we have some body which is capable of giving thought and study to the subject in an official way, such as a committee of the house.
It would be helpful also if' a committee of the house had an opportunity of direct contact with the officials of the department, many of whom have no doubt had much to do with framing the estimates now before us. It would be interesting to have the views of some of these officials at first hand and to question them. That would be of great assistance to members of the house in the discharge of their duties.
In concluding my remarks on that theme, I hope that the Minister of National Health and Welfare will be able to persuade his colleagues that the time has come when the rules of the house ought to be revised at least to the extent of providing for the estab-

Supply-Health and Welfare
lishment of a standing committee on health and welfare and social security; and, as I have said, I would include housing in it.
It is difficult to approach a review of the functions of this department without having an eye on the sometimes difficult question of the borderline of jurisdiction as between parliament on the one hand and the legislatures of the provinces on the other, in the field of public health and welfare. It is not my intention to precipitate a debate or discussion on the proposals submitted by the dominion government to the dominion-provincial conference. I believe that last year we did our best to assist those engaged in that conference, and those engaged in the meetings of the economic committee, between the two sessions of parliament, by refraining-as I described it on an earlier occasion

from muddying the waters of the conference. It is a matter of hope on the part of all of us that anything that is attempted in this field will be done in the spirit of cooperation, but I do lay stress on one or two principles in this respect. I am sure the minister has them in mind, but they are principles of leading importance in this field.
Due recognition must be given not only to the constitutional prerogatives of the provinces, as those -which possess jurisdiction in the field of administration of health and welfare services under the constitution, but also to the desirability of keeping our practice close to that constitutional position. I think it is axiomatic that we shall have the best administration of health services and the best administration of welfare services as well if the governments immediately responsible for such administration are those closest to the people. It has always been my view that the closer the administration is to the people concerned in the fields of health and welfare, the better will be our administration, the more efficient, and the closer .it will approach its objective of meeting direct and proven social needs.
With that in mind, I urge that, apart from those specialized fields which the constitution vests in the dominion, such as quarantine and the health of civil servants and so on, we must avoid overlapping as between the dominion and the provincial administrations.
We shall do well, in the second place, to avoid centralization. The fathers of confederation are sometimes not given justice. There is a feeling on the part of some that there is more wisdom in the year 1946 than there was in the year 1867. The fathers of confederation exercised vision and foresight when they devised a constitution which places the administration of health and welfare services under
the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures. If we avoid overlapping on the one hand and centralization on the other, I think we shall avoid waste and duplication.
Let us at all times seek to keep administration in the fields of health and welfare close to the people. Let us, in approaching these twin fields appropriately linked in one department, ever keep before us the imperative necessity of maintaining close cooperation between the dominion and the provinces. The act under which the minister administers his department recognizes the limited field assigned to the dominion by the constitution in these matters. The principal functions assigned to the department under the act of 1944, establishing this department, are, with the exception' of those specialized fields I mentioned a moment ago, research and assistance to the provinces with information. There is useful work to be done in those fields, but I urge that the dominion will make its best contribution to national health and welfare if it has due regard for the constitution.

speechtext: Would the minister care to make a general statement regarding the first item? It might be mentioned that his department has prepared three useful studies in the whole field of health services during the last few years, and I am sure that the people whose interest in health was aroused by these studies expected that some constructive steps would have been under way by this time had the dominion-provincial conference been more successful. I personally would appreciate some statement by the minister regarding future plans, since seven of the nine provinces were prepared to reach some agreement with the federal authority with minor adjustments. It might not be too much to expect that the federal government might be prepared to enter into negotiations with some or all of these seven provinces in the fields in which there has been some general agreement. Would the minister make some statement regarding plans as to where we go from here?

In answer to the hon. member who has just taken his seat, I would refer to the statement of the Prime Minister of May 9, which appears at page 1345 of Hansard. He was asked for a statement on the dominion-provincial conference, and he said that a discussion on that and of the developments that were necessary would be entered on by the Minister of Finance when he came to present his budget. I am afraid that any discussion I entered on now would be in anticipation of that. Unless the hon. member has some matters particularly related
Supply-Health and Welfare

to health and welfare, such as the health pro-prosals that form part of the dominion governments proposals to the provinces, I am afraid I might be anticipating something that more properly might be entered on later. However, if there are any points he would like to have answered as to the attitude of the government, the course of the discussions in the conference and the meaning of the dominion government's proposals on health and welfare as made to the conference, I should be only too glad to go into them just as fully as the committee might wish.
With regard to the remarks of the hon. member for Eglinton, he expressed regret that he did not have a statement of expenditures to compare with the estimates. That, of course, is a comment that might be made about the estimates in any year and of any department. The statements of expenditures are not put in the estimates, but they are put in the public accounts, and the public accounts come out just as soon as they can be prepared.
The hon. member spoke about the desirability of comparing expenses in this department in a previous year with the estimates for this year. I regret that that is not possible because there are no expenditures for a full previous year. The department was not in full operation for a full year before; therefore, there are not any comparable figures even to be found on reference to the public accounts. He also referred to the fact that the last report for the department is for the year ended March 31, 1945. That report is furnished to parliament in accordance with section 11 of the act. It was tabled well in advance of the time that might have been usual, and the report for the year ended March 31, 1946, will be tabled in due course in accordance with the act.
The hon. member referred to his own suggestion made in a motion which he had on the order paper that a special committee should be-

speechtext:
-a standing committee should be provided for in the rules to deal with matters of health and welfare. That suggestion might very properly be made to the special committee which is advising Mr. Speaker on the rules of the house. I am sure that if the committee reports in favour of the establishment of such a standing committee the government will have to give serious consideration to that report. I must say that my own idea with regard to this some

time ago was that there should be such a standing committee; but on considering the matter and looking into the practice in the United States and in England, I am coming to the view that it probably would be a mistake for us to have a number of standing committees dealing with the functions of different departments, such as they have in the United States. That leads to a totally different parliamentary system, one which is very much more similar to that in force in the United States than that on which we have modeled our own parliamentary system, namely, the parliament at Westminster, where they have no functional committees. They have five standing committees, and matters are referred to one or another of the committees by Mr. Speaker. From such examination as I have made of it, and comments made in England, I believe that the British procedure is the best; that the multiplication of functional committees in the United States leads to an effort by committees to administer departments. I believe that experience has shown that our system is as good as, if not better than, any in the world. Therefore, on that point, on which I have an open mind, I certainly am not convinced that we should change. I think we should consider most cautiously the institution of standing committees which have a definite relationship with the department and to which estimates would regularly be referred.
With regard to the hon. member's comments on the constitutional position, of course we are fully alive to that. Under the provisions of the constitution the primary responsibility for health and welfare generally rests with the provinces. Paragraph 7 of section 92 of the British North America Act gives power to the provincial legislatures to enact laws in relation to:
The establishment, maintenance, and management of hospitals, asylums, charities, and eleemosynary institutions in and for the province, other than marine hospitals.
When the hon. member suggests that there should be no overlapping and that we should each exercise jurisdiction within our appropriate fields, I should like to ask him what functions of the department he would like to see estopped. Would he suggest that the family allowances provision, the old age pension provision-
